_doc: Fact registry. Each entry: the claim as we teach it, its status, sources, and machine rules. 'forbid' patterns fail the script and/or on-screen text (scope). 'hedge' requires one of the hedge words within the same turn or the `window` turns before it. A line tagged {trap} is exempt from forbid rules (it is a deliberate mistake that the next turn corrects). 'visual' entries auto-generate an on-screen beat (e.g. a range bar) where the trigger phrase is spoken. 'require' rules apply to script kinds listed in `kinds` (default: all).

facts.claim: Syphilis may have crossed from the Americas to Europe; the origin is debated (Columbian vs pre-Columbian hypotheses).
sources: premium2027 ch03 (states it flatly; we hedge)
Harper et al. 2011; Majander et al. 2020 (contested genetic evidence)

facts.claim: Portuguese traders brought maize to Africa in the 1500s, where it became a staple; it reached Ming China and South Asia by the 1600s.
Madeira and São Tomé ran sugar plantations on enslaved African labor before the Americas did; the model crossed the Atlantic.
Many Europeans, especially in the north, were wary of tomatoes (nightshade family) and grew them as curiosities before eating them widely.
Almost all domesticated livestock went west; the turkey (domesticated in Mesoamerica) went east.
Sugarcane (the plant) went west; sugar (the commodity) flowed east to Europe.
Enslaved Africans were in the Americas by c. 1502; Potosí silver began in 1545. Chains predate silver.
sources: Bakewell, Miners of the Red Mountain (1984)

facts.claim: Portuguese Brazil was the largest single destination of the trans-Atlantic slave trade; the Caribbean collectively was comparable. Spain alone is the wrong frame.

forbid.why: Brazil and the Caribbean were the main sugar destinations

facts.claim: Spain coerced Native labor (encomienda) before and alongside the turn to enslaved African labor.

require.why: the labor story must name encomienda before the African labor shift

facts.claim: African states and merchants sold captives to European traders; the trade involved African political actors, not only European ships.
sources: Thornton, Africa and Africans in the Making of the Atlantic World (1998)

require.why: Africans must appear as actors, not only cargo

facts.claim: Estimates of Native population loss run roughly 50–90% between 1500 and 1650; 8–9 of 10 applies to the hardest-hit towns, not the hemisphere.

hedge.trigger: \b(eight|8) or (nine|9) (out )?of (ten|10)\b|\bnine out of ten\b|\b9 (out )?of 10\b|\bnine in ten\b|\b9 in 10\b

visual.label: NATIVE POPULATION LOST, 1500–1650
visual.caption: Estimates run roughly 50–90%. Hardest-hit towns: 8 or 9 of 10.

facts.claim: The Florentine Codex was compiled under Bernardino de Sahagún with Nahua informants, decades after 1520. Our account is a paraphrase.
Enslaved Africans were present in Hispaniola by c. 1502; the trade began with sugar, not cotton; 1619 is not the start.

forbid.why: slavery in the Americas predates Jamestown by a century

facts.claim: The Black Death was flea/rodent-borne, not a herd-animal crowd disease; use 'epidemics', not 'plagues', when setting up the virgin-soil explanation.

forbid.why: invites the Black Death, which the herd-animal answer doesn't explain

facts.claim: Disease led the conquest but did not work alone (war, enslavement, Native allies, collapse of food systems).

forbid.why: the Spanish neither aimed nor understood the epidemics
syphilis is contested; say 'almost entirely one way'

facts.claim: Evaluating the Exchange requires both halves: European gains, American losses, and American gains (horse, wheat, cattle).
